definition: The first ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state, forming gaseous 1+ ions, as in $\ce{Na(g) -> Na^+(g) + e-}$; it is always positive.
The reduction in the nucleus's pull on an outer electron, caused by repulsion from the electrons in inner energy levels.
The net positive charge an outer electron feels once shielding by the inner electrons is allowed for, roughly the number of protons minus the number of inner electrons.
Half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element; it generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
An element of group 1 other than hydrogen, such as sodium or potassium: a reactive metal with one valence electron that forms 1+ ions.
An element of group 17; fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are reactive non-metals with seven valence electrons that form 1− ions.
An element of group 18, such as helium, neon or argon: a very unreactive gas of single atoms, whose outer sublevels are full.
The repeating pattern in properties such as atomic radius and ionization energy across each period and down each group of the periodic table.
The energy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms to form gaseous 1− ions, as in $\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl^-(g)}$; it is negative (energy is released) for most elements.
